key_insight: Anchoring — adding a simple penalty that pulls independently trained predictors toward a common reference — can provably and practically reduce model disagreement (expected squared prediction difference) while controlling the usual training parameters like regularization and sample size.
problem_solved: Reduces unpredictable divergence between independently trained models (model disagreement), which undermines reliability, reproducibility, and downstream decision-making when models are trained without coordination.
method: Formalize model disagreement as the expected squared difference in real-valued predictions between two models trained on independent data.
Introduce an anchoring mechanism: add a proximal/regularization term that ties each model to a common anchor (e.g., a reference predictor, public model, or averaged initialization) during training.
Provide theoretical bounds and empirical evaluation showing disagreement falls as anchor strength (and/or sample size/regularization) increases, with explicit trade-offs against predictive accuracy.
impact: Gives practitioners a simple, tunable tool to make independent training runs more consistent without heavy coordination — improving reproducibility, safer model updates, and more stable ensemble or multi-stakeholder deployment.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: two independently trained models with large prediction gaps vs. two anchored models with aligned predictions.
Line chart: disagreement (y) vs. anchor strength or sample size (x) showing monotonic decrease and a small accuracy trade-off curve.
Block diagram: training loop showing original loss + anchoring/proximal term highlighting the anchor source (public model, average, or prior).
Icon set: reliability (shield), reproducibility (repeat arrows), and trade-off (scale) to summarize benefits and costs.
paper_authors: Eric Eaton, Surbhi Goel, Marcel Hussing, Michael Kearns, Aaron Roth
